\begin{abstract}

Indirect memory access (IMA), where one load's address depends on another load's returned data (e.g., $A[B[i]]$), is a major performance bottleneck for graph analytics and sparse linear algebra on GPUs, causing the majority of L1 cache misses. While CPU architects have developed effective IMA prefetchers, their single-threaded assumptions prevent adoption on massively multithreaded GPUs. Meanwhile, existing GPU prefetchers rely on stride-based patterns and cannot handle data-dependent accesses.

We propose GRASP (GPU Register-chain Aware Sector Prefetcher), a hardware prefetcher that exploits a structural property of GPU's SASS ISA: the \texttt{IMAD.WIDE} instruction directly exposes IMA parameters---scale, base address, and index value---as instruction operands, enabling zero-inference detection. GRASP identifies \texttt{LDG}$\to$\texttt{IMAD.WIDE}$\to$\texttt{LDG} dependency chains at the issue stage and employs a two-step index-then-data prefetch pipeline, with per-SM shared tables for training amortization and (base, scale) key merging to handle compiler-induced PC proliferation.

Evaluated on graph workloads with an A100 configuration in Accel-Sim, GRASP achieves a geomean IPC improvement of 35.5\% (up to 49.8\%), at a hardware cost of approximately 2.5\,KB per SM.

\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

% ¶1: IMA definition + universality
Graph analytics (e.g., social networks, road networks, web graphs),
sparse linear algebra, and data-intensive applications increasingly
rely on GPUs for acceleration~\cite{wang2016gunrock, xu2019gardenia,
yang2022graphblast, chen2020pangolin}.
A defining characteristic of these workloads is the \emph{indirect
memory access} (IMA) pattern \texttt{A[B[i]]}, in which one load's
address depends on the return value of a prior
load~\cite{yu2015imp, fu2024dmp}.
IMA fundamentally breaks spatial and temporal locality: the data
array addresses are determined at runtime and scatter unpredictably
across memory~\cite{talati2021prodigy, xue2024tyche}.
Because this irregularity is inherent to the data structure---not an
artifact of poor layout---it cannot be eliminated by data
reordering~\cite{burtscher2012irregular, shi2018graph}.

% ¶2: IMA breaks GPU latency hiding + Prefetching opportunity + Fig 1
GPUs hide memory latency by interleaving thousands of concurrent
warps, yet IMA undermines this mechanism on two fronts.
First, IMA instructions contribute \textbf{61--93\% of all L1 data cache
misses} across six representative graph algorithms
(Figure~\ref{fig:cache-ima}, left), making them the dominant source
of pipeline stalls.
Second, the serial dependency between index and data loads doubles
the effective memory latency per access, inflating the number of
warps required for full latency hiding well beyond the hardware limit
of 64 warps per SM (\S\ref{sec:motivation}).
%
Crucially, however, a prefetching opportunity exists: while L1 miss
rates are high (38--59\%), L2 hit rates are also high (70--89\%),
indicating that the data \emph{resides in L2 but not in L1}
(Figure~\ref{fig:cache-ima}, left).
An ideal L1 data cache that eliminates all L1 misses achieves a
geometric mean speedup of \textbf{2.04$\times$} across 25~workload
configurations (Figure~\ref{fig:cache-ima}, right), confirming
substantial headroom for an L1-targeted prefetcher.

\begin{figure}[t]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/fig1_cache_ima_ideal.pdf}
  \caption{(a)~L1 miss rate decomposed into IMA data, IMA index, and
    non-IMA misses (stacked), alongside L2 miss rate (per-algorithm
    median, symmetric graphs).
    (b)~Ideal L1D speedup (geometric mean per algorithm; overall
    2.04$\times$ across 25 configurations).}
  \label{fig:cache-ima}
\end{figure}

% Transition to ¶3
This motivates GPU-specific prefetching for IMA---yet no existing GPU
prefetcher addresses this access pattern.

% ¶3: GPU stride prefetching — 15 years of progress, IMA blind spot
GPU prefetching has been studied for over 15~years, achieving
consistent gains on stride and streaming
patterns~\cite{lee2010manythread, jog2013orchestrated, oh2016apres,
koo2018caps, oh2018wasp, mostofi2023snake}.
These works progressively advanced from inter-thread
prefetching~\cite{lee2010manythread} and scheduling--prefetch
co-design~\cite{jog2013orchestrated}, to CTA-aware leading-warp
detection~\cite{koo2018caps} and variable-length stride
chains~\cite{mostofi2023snake}.
However, IMA requires a fundamentally different detection mechanism:
the data load address is determined by a runtime index value, not by
an arithmetic stride.
Indeed, CAPS explicitly skips data-dependent
accesses~\cite{koo2018caps}, and Snake's chains remain
stride-based~\cite{mostofi2023snake}.

% ¶4: CPU IMA prefetchers — proven effective but cannot migrate
Meanwhile, the CPU community has accumulated nearly a decade of
hardware IMA prefetching, demonstrating that the problem is tractable.
IMP detects \texttt{A[B[i]]} patterns via address
differentials~\cite{yu2015imp}, and the state-of-the-art
DMP~\cite{fu2024dmp} matches four classes of indirect patterns at
0.9\,KB.
Subsequent work has progressively addressed multi-level and
non-linear variants~\cite{cavus2020atp, kaushik2021gretch,
xue2024tyche, talati2021prodigy}.
Yet all these designs assume a single-threaded address stream with
per-core independent state~\cite{ainsworth2019indirect}---assumptions
that collapse under the 64-warp concurrency of a GPU SM,
where na\"{\i}ve per-warp replication would cost
57.6\,KB/SM (\S\ref{sec:motivation}).

% ¶5: Spare Register — sole GPU IMA attempt, decade-long void
The only hardware prefetcher targeting IMA on GPUs is Spare
Register~\cite{lakshminarayana2014spare}, which detects load-pairs
via value-tag propagation and stores prefetched data in idle
registers, achieving 10\% average IPC improvement.
However, it was designed and evaluated on the Fermi
architecture~(2010)---whose cache hierarchy and warp scheduling
differ substantially from modern SM80+
designs.
In the decade since, every subsequent GPU prefetcher has targeted
stride patterns exclusively~\cite{koo2018caps, oh2018wasp,
mostofi2023snake}.

% Transition — zero-position landing
GPU IMA prefetching thus remains an open problem---one that demands a
detection approach native to the GPU's execution model.

% ¶6: IMAD.WIDE — the ISA structural advantage
Rather than migrating CPU techniques, we observe that the GPU's own
ISA provides a more direct path.
Specifically, NVIDIA's SASS instruction \texttt{IMAD.WIDE\;Rd,
Rindex, Rscale, c[base]} encodes \emph{all} the information needed
to prefetch the data load in an IMA chain:
the \emph{base address} of the data array (a kernel-lifetime constant
in constant memory), the \emph{scale factor} (element size, a
compile-time constant), and the \emph{index dependency} (the source
register linking to the preceding index load).
A single observation of this instruction suffices to extract every
prefetch parameter---with \textbf{zero inference}.
This structural guarantee arises because GPU pointers are 64-bit
while graph indices are typically 32-bit integers; the resulting
address computation (32$\times$32$+$64$\to$64) uniquely maps to
\texttt{IMAD.WIDE} in the SASS ISA, making it the compiler's
obligatory choice (\S\ref{sec:motivation}).
Across 12~algorithms compiled for six GPU generations
(Volta through Hopper), 9 of 12 algorithms exhibit $\geq$86\%
\texttt{IMAD.WIDE} conformance, confirming the pattern's
cross-architecture stability.

% ¶7: GRASP overview + selected results
Based on this insight, we propose \textbf{GRASP} (\textbf{G}PU
\textbf{R}egister-chain \textbf{A}ware \textbf{S}ector
\textbf{P}refetcher), which detects
\texttt{LDG$\to$IMAD.WIDE$\to$LDG} register dependency chains at
the issue stage and prefetches through a two-step
index-then-data pipeline.
GRASP's design inherits two structural advantages from
\texttt{IMAD.WIDE}: (1)~\emph{(base,\,scale) merging} collapses
60+ program counters in SpMV into $\sim$2 table entries, eliminating
PC-space explosion; and (2)~\emph{per-SM shared tables} amortize
training across 64~warps, requiring only $\sim$2.3\,KB/SM.
Evaluated on 28~workloads spanning 9~algorithms and 5~datasets,
GRASP achieves a geometric mean IPC improvement of \textbf{18\%}
(up to \textbf{122\%}) over an unmodified A100 configuration.

% ¶8: Contributions
\smallskip\noindent
This paper makes the following contributions:
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*, nosep]
\item \textbf{IMA Characterization and IMAD.WIDE Discovery.}
  We present the first systematic quantification of IMA behavior on
  modern GPUs, showing that IMA accounts for 61--93\% of L1 misses
  with an ideal L1D headroom of 2.04$\times$ (geometric mean).
  We identify \texttt{IMAD.WIDE} as a structurally guaranteed ISA
  feature that encodes all IMA prefetch parameters, stable across
  six GPU generations.
\item \textbf{GRASP Design.}
  We propose a zero-inference IMA prefetcher built on
  \texttt{IMAD.WIDE} detection, featuring an index--data two-step
  pipeline, (base,\,scale) merging, and per-SM shared tables at
  $\sim$2.3\,KB/SM---the first dedicated IMA prefetcher for modern
  GPUs.
\item \textbf{Comprehensive Evaluation.}
  We evaluate GRASP on 28~workloads across three SOTA GPU
  prefetcher baselines (Snake, CAPS, Spare Register),
  demonstrating consistent IPC improvements with a geometric mean
  of 18\% (up to 122\%).
\end{itemize}

\section{Key Insight: ISA-Exposed IMA Structure}
\label{sec:insight}

\textit{[IMAD.WIDE exposes scale, base, index as instruction operands — zero-inference detection. Structural guarantee: IMAD.WIDE is the only single-instruction 32×32+64→64 in SASS, compiler will not choose 3-instruction alternative. See insight.md Insight~1.]}

\label{sec:design}

\subsection{Overview}
\textit{[Architecture figure (Fig.~\ref{fig:grasp-arch}) — CD/CT/TT/IPU/DPU/PRB/ACU/TC in cache hierarchy. Two-step prefetch: index first, then data.]}

\subsection{Chain Detection (CD)}
\textit{[Monitor issue stage for LDG→IMAD.WIDE→LDG. Extract (index\_PC, data\_PC, base, scale). Write CT + TT entries.]}

\subsection{Stride Learning (IST)}
\textit{[Per-PC iteration stride tracking. Convergence in 2--3 observations. Cross-kernel persistence.]}

\subsection{Index Prefetch (IPU)}
\textit{[On demand index load: compute prefetch\_addr = addr + stride × distance. Allocate PRB entry.]}

\subsection{Data Prefetch (DPU + ACU)}
\textit{[On index fill: ACU reads returned value, computes data\_addr = base + value × scale. DPU issues data prefetch.]}

\subsection{Throttle Control (TC)}
\textit{[MSHR utilization monitoring. Suppress prefetch when saturated.]}
